items.text: A Detroit homeowner hires a restoration contractor for flood repairs, not knowing his residential builder's license had been revoked. Under Epps v 4 Quarters Restoration, is that contract void or voidable?

C. Voidable, valid unless and until the homeowner elects to void it — Epps, 498 Mich 518 (2015), held that contracts between an innocent homeowner and an unlicensed builder are voidable, not void, overruling older 'void' language from cases like Stokes v Millen Roofing.
An unlicensed restoration contractor is sued by a homeowner for shoddy work. Can the contractor raise substantive defenses under MCL 339.2412(1)?

A. Yes, the statute only bars the contractor's own suit to collect compensation, not its ability to defend — Epps described MCL 339.2412(1) as a shield, not a sword: it removes the unlicensed contractor's power to sue, not its power to defend.
Under MCL 339.2412(3), can an unlicensed contractor who was unlicensed during performance impose a construction lien on the homeowner's property?

D. No, the statute bars imposing a lien if the person was unlicensed during the performance of the act or contract — MCL 339.2412(3) bars an unlicensed person from imposing or taking legal action to impose a lien on real property for work performed while unlicensed.

A homeowner in Grand Rapids signed a written residential repair contract that never states the contractor's license number, though the contractor is actually licensed. Under MCL 570.1114, can the contractor record a valid construction lien if unpaid?

D. No, the contract must state the license number to preserve residential lien rights — MCL 570.1114 requires the written contract to state that the contractor is licensed and the contractor's license number; omitting the number defeats residential lien rights.
A plumbing subcontractor first furnishes labor on a Livonia restoration job on May 1. Under MCL 570.1109(1), by what date must it serve a Notice of Furnishing?
C. May 21 (20 days) — MCL 570.1109(1) requires a subcontractor or supplier to serve a notice of furnishing within 20 days after furnishing the first labor or material.

A general contractor with a contract directly with the homeowner performs restoration work in Ann Arbor. Does it need to serve a Notice of Furnishing under MCL 570.1109 to preserve its own lien rights?

D. No, a contractor with a direct contract with the owner is not required to serve one — MCL 570.1109(1)'s final sentence exempts a contractor in direct contract with the owner from serving a notice of furnishing; only subs, suppliers, and laborers need to.
A restoration contractor last furnished labor on a Flint home on August 1. Under MCL 570.1111(1), by what date must it record a claim of lien to preserve lien rights?
B. October 30 (90 days) — MCL 570.1111(1) requires recording a claim of lien within 90 days after the lien claimant's last furnishing of labor or material; 90 days after August 1 is October 30.
A contractor recorded a claim of lien on a Saginaw home on March 1. Under MCL 570.1117(1), by what date must it file suit to enforce the lien through foreclosure?
A. March 1 of the following year (1 year) — MCL 570.1117(1) requires foreclosure proceedings to be brought no later than 1 year after the date the claim of lien was recorded.

A homeowner requests a sworn statement from her contractor before making final payment on a Kalamazoo restoration job. Under MCL 570.1110, what must the contractor provide, and what is the consequence of lying on it?

B. A sworn statement listing every sub, supplier, and unpaid laborer with amounts due; a false statement given with intent to defraud is a crime — MCL 570.1110 requires a sworn statement on demand, listing subs, suppliers, and unpaid laborers with amounts due; giving a false sworn statement with intent to defraud is a crime under the statute.

A homeowner's fire insurance policy contains an anti-assignment clause requiring the insurer's written consent for any assignment. After the fire, she assigns her already-accrued claim to a restoration contractor without the insurer's consent. Under Roger Williams Ins Co v Carrington (1880), is the assignment enforceable?

D. Yes, because an assignment made after the loss did not require the insurer's consent, and the anti-assignment clause is invalid as to the transfer of an accrued cause of action — Roger Williams Ins Co v Carrington, 43 Mich 252 (1880), held that a post-loss assignment did not require the insurer's consent and that the anti-assignment clause is invalid as applied to an accrued cause of action.
In Jawad A. Shah, M.D., PC v State Farm (2018), the Michigan Court of Appeals held that State Farm's anti-assignment clause was unenforceable against the healthcare providers' assignment because:

B. The assignment was of an accrued claim made after the loss, and enforcing the clause in that circumstance would violate public policy under Roger Williams v Carrington — Shah, 324 Mich App 182 (2018), held the clause unenforceable specifically because the assignment was of an already-accrued claim made after the loss, applying the public-policy rule from Roger Williams v Carrington, not an ambiguity or waiver theory.

A contractor holding an assignment of benefits sues an insurer for a claim paid 90 days late and asks the court to award the MCL 500.2006(4) 12% penalty interest directly to the contractor as its own independent statutory right. Is there published Michigan property case law supporting this exact position?

B. No, no published Michigan property case squarely holds that a contractor-assignee is 'a person directly entitled to benefits' in its own right — No published Michigan property-insurance case resolves whether a contractor-assignee counts as 'a person directly entitled to benefits' under MCL 500.2006(4); the safer position is that the contractor pursues the interest derivatively through the insured's right.

A restoration company with an AOB tells a homeowner it will negotiate the disputed portion of her claim directly with the carrier's adjuster for a fee equal to 20% of any additional amount recovered. Which Michigan statute makes this problematic regardless of the AOB?

A. MCL 500.1222, which requires an adjuster license to adjust a loss for compensation — Negotiating a disputed claim for a contingent fee is adjusting a loss for compensation, which requires an adjuster license under MCL 500.1222; an AOB does not create an exception to this licensing requirement.

A homeowner in Oakland County sues her insurer under the Michigan Consumer Protection Act, alleging the insurer's 2026 claims-handling practices were unfair and deceptive under chapter 20 of the Insurance Code. Under current MCL 445.904(3), what is the likely outcome?

C. The MCPA claim is barred, because MCL 445.904(3) bars an MCPA cause of action for chapter-20 conduct occurring on or after March 28, 2001 — MCL 445.904(3) bars the MCPA from applying to or creating a cause of action for chapter-20 insurance-code conduct occurring on or after March 28, 2001; the 1999 Smith v Globe Life carve-out that allowed such a claim has since been closed by this amendment.
What was the actual basis on which the plaintiff's MCPA claim against the insurer survived in Smith v Globe Life Ins Co (1999)?

B. The version of MCL 445.904(2) then in force expressly permitted a private action under section 11 for chapter-20-type conduct, a carve-out later closed by amendment — Smith v Globe Life Ins Co, 460 Mich 446 (1999), held the claim survived because the then-current §4(2) expressly permitted a private action under §11; that carve-out has since been closed by later statutory amendment, now reflected in MCL 445.904(3).
A contractor is owed $6,800 by a homeowner in Kent County for an unpaid restoration balance. Which Michigan court division has jurisdiction without either side needing an attorney, absent removal?

D. Small claims division, since $6,800 is under the current $7,000 limit — MCL 600.8401 sets the current small claims jurisdictional limit at $7,000, effective January 1, 2024, and $6,800 falls within it; MCL 600.8408(1) bars attorneys on both sides absent removal.
A collection agency wants to represent a homeowner in a small claims dispute with a contractor. Under MCL 600.8408(1), is this permitted?

C. No, a collection agency or its agent or employee is barred from taking part in small claims litigation — MCL 600.8408(1) expressly bars a collection agency or agent or employee of a collection agency, along with attorneys (except pro se), from taking part in filing, prosecuting, or defending small claims litigation.

A homeowner signs a $2,500 home improvement installment contract with a restoration contractor on a Friday, financing the balance through the contractor. Under MCL 445.1202(c)(4), by when must she rescind to use the HIFA right?

A. 5 p.m. on the following Monday, the next business day — MCL 445.1202(c)(4) gives a HIFA rescission right until 5 p.m. on the business day following the date of the contract; since Friday's next business day is Monday, that is the deadline, not 3 business days (that is the separate HSSA window).
A door-to-door storm-damage solicitor signs a homeowner to a full roof contract at her home on a Tuesday, with no emergency and no handwritten waiver. Under MCL 445.112(1), by when can she cancel?

A. Midnight of the following Friday, the third business day after signing — MCL 445.112(1) gives a home-solicitation buyer the right to cancel until midnight of the third business day after signing; Tuesday plus 3 business days is midnight Friday.
A mitigation company wants to invoke the HSSA emergency exception under MCL 445.112(5) to begin extraction immediately. Which of these is NOT one of the three required conditions?

C. The contractor must be a licensed adjuster under MCL 500.1222 — MCL 445.112(5)'s three conditions are substantial good-faith performance, a separate handwritten dated and signed waiver statement, and (for goods) inability to return them in as-good condition; adjuster licensure is unrelated to this HSSA exception.
